query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal exposure in the service regime triggers the metastable, single-phase Mg-containing HEA to decompose via heterogeneous nucleation, forming finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that initially promote a coherent, protective MgO scale at high temperature. However, upon further coarsening of these precipitates, localized Mg depletion in the matrix degrades the oxide scale adherence and increases corrosion rates.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state of a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Thermal aging (annealing) under controlled conditions in a neutral/inert environment at service-relevant temperatures.
generation.conditions: Heat treatments performed at temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) and times spanning the early transformation (short aging) to overaging (extended aging) regimes, reflecting typical high-temperature service boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely dispersed, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that nucleate heterogeneously within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation enhances Mg diffusion enabling the nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Initially, the formation of fine precipitates favors the development of a coherent MgO protective layer, improving oxidation and corrosion resistance. As aging continues, precipitate coarsening leads to local Mg depletion in the matrix, ultimately undermining the integrity of the protective oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Short-duration aging produces a fine precipitate distribution, retaining or even enhancing the protective oxide layer and corrosion resistance compared to the initial metastable state. In contrast, prolonged aging results in coarser intermetallics, reduced matrix Mg content, and a corresponding decline in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.baseline: The initial state with a homogeneous metastable solid-solution microstructure lacking distinct intermetallic phases.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects occur within a critical time-temperature window (service-relevant conditions up to about 800°C and short aging times). Beyond this regime, precipitate coarsening undermines protection.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature and time thresholds for the transition from protective to detrimental microstructures remain to be quantified; the specific intermetallic phase compositions and their kinetics are also not fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of the Mg-containing HEA. Subject one set to short-duration aging within the service temperature range and another set to extended aging under identical conditions. Perform controlled comparisons using identical processing and measurement protocols.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to determine precipitate size, distribution, and phase composition
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to assess corrosion rate
High-temperature oxidation measurements (e.g., TGA or oxide scale analysis) to evaluate oxide scale formation and kinetics
Chemical mapping (e.g., EDS or atom probe tomography) to monitor local Mg concentration changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon extended aging, there is no observable coarsening of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (or if only fine precipitates form across all times) and no corresponding degradation in corrosion or oxidation resistance when compared to the short-aged state, then the hypothesis is falsified.
